title: Insight goes west
hookLine: Burmese and Thai meditation methods reach Western lay students

cards: Falling. In a meditation hall in Yangon, a student sits with her attention on her belly, silently naming each movement as the breath comes and goes. A sound outside: hearing.
A thought about lunch: thinking. Back to rising, falling. Her teacher's instruction is short: know what is happening, while it's happening.
No robes required, no years in a monastery first. That simple method, and other ways of sitting from Burma and Thailand, traveled to lay students on the other side of the world.

teach.b: In Burma, teachers began to teach meditation to ordinary laypeople, not only to monks and nuns.
Ledi Sayadaw wrote and taught for lay students, and later Mahasi Sayadaw opened a center in Yangon where anyone could come and practice.
The Mahasi way is noting: a soft mental label for whatever is happening, moment by moment. It rests on an old teaching, the sutta on the setting up of mindfulness.

There, the Buddha says a practitioner who is walking knows, I am walking, and who is standing knows, I am standing, and so with sitting and lying down. Know the body as body, feelings as feelings, the mind as mind.
The Pali for the clear seeing that grows from this is vipassana, insight.
In Thailand, forest monks like Ajahn Chah taught in simple monasteries among the trees. Western men came to him, ordained, and some went on to found monasteries in England and elsewhere.
And Western students who had sat in Burma, Thailand and India came home and taught insight meditation in plain retreat centers, often to people who called themselves nothing in particular.

The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words, opens its chapter on earnestness like this: "Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvâna), thoughtlessness the path of death." Rising, falling, hearing, thinking.
Small, earnest noting, carried across the world.

how: Insight meditation students sit and walk in silence, noting what arises, often on retreats at centers in the Burmese or Thai lineages, and Theravada monasteries in the West also teach meditation to laypeople.

games.q: you're meditating, noting rising and falling, and a thought about lunch shows up. what does the method say to do?
o: note thinking, then come back to rising and falling.
follow the thought to see where it goes.
games.why: in noting, you give the thought a soft label, thinking, and return to the belly. nothing is fought.

practice: Rest your attention on your belly and note it softly as it moves: rising, falling; if a sound comes, note hearing, if a thought comes, note thinking, and come back.
Keep the labels gentle and short, like a whisper, with no need to get it right. Just know what is happening, while it's happening.
